arguments.heading: YES ON I: KEEP THE PROMISE. AFFORDABLE HOUSING WITH NO NEW TAXES.
arguments.text: San Francisco’s housing crisis is pushing families, seniors, teachers, nurses, artists, immigrants, and young people out of the city they love. In 2020, voters approved a tax on the sale of properties worth more than $10 million, specifically so that money could fund affordable housing and rent relief. It worked until politicians ignored the will of voters. This tax on San Francisco’s wealthiest property owners provided emergency rent relief to more than 10,000 households and helped preserve and build hundreds of affordable homes. But it wasn’t guaranteed. In the past two years, none of this revenue has gone to affordable housing. Prop I will finally keep the promise and implement the measure voters approved. • Doesn’t raise taxes -- uses only revenue from a tax voters already approved. • Cuts the transfer tax for new housing construction, so we keep building the homes we need. • Independent oversight -- mandatory annual audits by the City Controller, filed publicly. • The only measure on the ballot that guarantees both innovative social housing and ongoing rental assistance. This November, San Franciscans have a historic opportunity: two measures on the ballot that guarantee affordable housing funding without raising anyone’s taxes. Vote YES on Prop I to guarantee this funding finally does what voters intended. Read more: YesonISF.com

authors: San Francisco Building and Construction Trades Council
arguments.heading: DON’T BE FOOLED: PROP I CREATES A NONPROFIT SLUSH FUND AND DOESN’T GUARANTEE NEW HOUSING
arguments.text: Prop I’s proponents say this measure “keeps the promise” of affordable housing without raising taxes. That is not what Prop I does. Prop I would lock roughly $120 million a year away from the General Fund without requiring that a single new unit of housing be built. 30% must go to “social housing.” Another 25% can go to nonprofits to buy existing apartments. Another 10% can fund nonprofit programs that do not build new homes. Five percent can go to administration. That means at least 70% of the money does not have to build housing. Audits do not fix Prop I’s fundamental flaw. It can be perfectly audited and still spend most of its money without building a single new home. A transfer-tax cut does not change that. How much new housing does Prop I require? None. The budget damage goes further. Pulling $120 million out of the General Fund shrinks funding baselines, including Muni’s. Amid a Muni funding crisis, Prop I would drastically cut transit funding while reducing resources for firefighters, public safety, clean streets, and other essential services. The San Francisco Building and Construction Trades Council represents workers who actually build housing. We support affordable housing, not a measure that promises housing without guaranteeing new homes. Vote NO on Prop I.

arguments.text: Vote NO on the Affordable Housing Guarantee Act. While affordable housing is an important priority, locking transfer tax revenues into rigid set-asides is fiscal mismanagement that threatens San Francisco’s financial stability. 1. Creates Dangerous Budget Earmarks San Francisco’s General Fund pays for vital everyday services—including police officers, firefighters, 911 dispatchers, street cleaning, and public parks. Carving out transfer tax revenues into a restricted fund starves the General Fund of essential dollars, forcing severe service cuts across the city during lean budget years. 2. Relies on Highly Volatile Revenue Real estate transfer taxes are notoriously unpredictable. Basing housing commitments on real estate sales creates an unstable funding cycle that collapses whenever property values or commercial transactions drop. Managing long-term programs on volatile tax revenues is fiscally reckless. 3. Deepens Downtown Economic Stagnation San Francisco’s commercial real estate market is already struggling with historically high vacancy rates. Increasing burden or restricting tax policy on high-value properties discourages investment, depresses property values, and weakens our overall tax base—ultimately reducing total revenue available for public services. 4. Reduces Flexibility and Oversight City leaders need the flexibility to adapt to economic downturns and emerging local emergencies. Tying revenue up in permanent structural mandates removes budget oversight and prevents the City from reallocating resources where they are needed most. Protect core city services and financial stability. Vote NO on Measure I.

arguments.heading: YES ON I — AFFORDABLE HOUSING. NO NEW TAXES.
arguments.text: Opponents call affordable housing “an important priority.” They’re right. But they oppose Prop I, which builds affordable housing without raising taxes. That’s plain wrong. San Francisco’s state-mandated housing plan calls for 46,000 affordable homes to be built by 2031. Prop I is a step forward. It will create thousands of affordable homes without costing taxpayers a dime. Prop I keeps a promise made to voters in 2020 which city hall politicians have ignored. It requires the city to use an existing tax on sales of properties valued at ten million dollars or more to fund affordable housing. For the first few years, politicians kept the promise. But over the last two years, not one dollar of this revenue has gone to housing. Prop I is accountable: • Every dollar in Prop I will be managed by the Mayor’s Office of Housing • Mandatory annual audits will be conducted by the City Controller • Taxes on new housing are reduced to encourage growth • And it won’t raise taxes! Our housing crisis demands innovative solutions, not tired opposition from people who have opposed affordable housing for decades. Join us and Vote Yes on I.

arguments.heading: Pissed Off Voters Agree: Vote HELL YES! on Prop I
arguments.text: Make real estate investors pay their fair share so we can make San Francisco more affordable! Hold up, didn’t we already vote on this in 2020? Yup. And we’re pissed off at City Hall for ignoring the will of the voters. San Francisco voters originally passed Prop I in 2020, which taxed high-dollar real estate sales: 5% for properties over $10 million, and 6% for properties over $25 million. And Prop I won by a landslide, raising nearly $500 million from luxury real estate sales since it passed in 2020. Only a quarter of that funding has actually been dedicated to preserving and developing affordable housing. City Hall has ignored the will of the voters and withheld the remaining funding. NOT cool! So now Prop I is back to make sure that this time City Hall can’t ignore the voters or our five-alarm affordability crisis! Voting yes on Prop I guarantees City Hall must spend that luxury real estate tax money on affordable housing, as it was intended. Do you agree that big-money real estate sales should be taxed to fund affordable housing? Vote HELL YES! on Prop I Read our voter guide: https://theLeagueSF.org

arguments.heading: RENTS ARE UP 22%. FRONT-LINE HOUSING GROUPS AGREE: YES ON I
arguments.text: As organizations working on the front lines of San Francisco’s housing crisis, we meet seniors choosing between rent and medicine, families doubling up because they can’t afford an apartment alone, young people wondering if they’ll ever be able to build a future here, and workers who keep our city running but can’t afford to live in it. We are living through a housing emergency. This year alone, median rent for a one-bedroom hit an all-time high of $4,060 -- up 21.9%, the steepest jump of any major U.S. city, according to Zumper. We support Yes on I because it funds what works: Building permanently affordable homes, providing rental assistance before families lose their housing, and creating new housing that remains affordable for generations. Prop I makes sure this existing revenue is permanently dedicated to affordable housing, innovative social housing for people across a range of incomes, and rent relief. It does not raise taxes, and it cuts the transfer tax in half for new housing construction to support the production of the homes our city needs. Vote YES on Prop I and help make San Francisco a city where everyone has the opportunity to thrive.

arguments.heading: NEIGHBORHOOD HOMEOWNERS: YES ON I IS A FAIR AND SENSIBLE HOUSING SOLUTION
arguments.text: Voting Yes on I is a simple choice: funding for affordable housing and rent relief, with no new taxes for anyone -- including homeowners. Prop I dedicates an existing tax on luxury property sales over $10 million to affordable housing and rent relief. Rental assistance allows struggling tenants to get back on their feet without small landlords footing the bill. • No taxes for homeowners -- this measure applies only to sellers of $10 million-plus properties. • Independent oversight -- mandatory annual audits by the City Controller, with public reporting to the Board of Supervisors. • No funding for administrators’ salaries or pensions -- money for housing and rent relief, not bureaucracy. Vote YES on Proposition I to build strong, stable neighborhoods at no cost to homeowners.

arguments.heading: BLACK LEADERS SUPPORT YES ON I
arguments.text: San Francisco’s strength is its diversity, but decades of displacement have taken a devastating toll on our community. Our Black population has declined from 13.5% in the 1970s to just 5% today. We continue to bear a disproportionate share of the housing crisis. It’s urgent that we repair the harm of decades of redevelopment, displacement, and discriminatory housing policies that pushed communities of color out of San Francisco. As African American leaders, we stand united in our support for Proposition I so working and middle class families can put down roots and continue to contribute to San Francisco. Vote YES on Prop I.

arguments.heading: LATINO LEADERS SAY YES ON I BECAUSE WORKING FAMILIES BELONG HERE
arguments.text: The Latino community keeps San Francisco’s economy running -- and working families belong here. While Latinos make up just 15% of the city’s population, they represent more than 30% of its workforce, filling essential roles in healthcare, hospitality, construction, food service, and other industries that our city depends on every day. Yet far too many Latino families are being priced out. More than half of Latino households spend over one-third of their income on rent, leaving them rent-burdened and struggling to make ends meet. Prop I will build more affordable homes for low- and middle-income San Franciscans, giving working families the opportunity to put down roots, build stability, and keep contributing to the communities they call home. Vote YES on I.

arguments.heading: YES, YES ON HOUSING: LET’S BUILD THE HOUSING WE NEED
arguments.text: This year, San Francisco has an opportunity to pass two historic affordable housing measures that will make a tremendous difference for our city -- without raising a penny of taxes. Yes on I is vital to achieving our housing goals: • Provides funding for housing without raising taxes • Reduces the transfer tax currently paid by large new housing projects, encouraging housing growth at all income levels • Establishes innovative social housing which would help address the housing needs of middle income residents and gives people from different walks of life an opportunity to afford homes and build community together • Helps San Francisco meet our state-mandated affordable housing goals, avoiding state penalties We urge you to vote YES, YES ON HOUSING. Vote YES on I.

arguments.heading: JOIN SAN FRANCISCO FIREFIGHTERS IN OPPOSING PROP I’S DIVERSION OF GENERAL FUND SERVICES
arguments.text: San Francisco should not put essential emergency services under greater budget pressure for a measure that does not guarantee new affordable housing. Prop I would pull roughly $120 million every year from the General Fund and place it into a dedicated non-profit slush fund. Those are dollars the City currently has flexibility to use for firefighters, paramedics, emergency response, clean streets, public safety, transit, and other essential services. Firefighters know what happens when City budgets tighten: departments are asked to do more with less while staffing, equipment, and emergency-response systems face greater pressure. Do not create another budget hole without actually guaranteeing new affordable housing. Protect essential services. Vote NO on Prop I.

arguments.heading: Vote NO on I: Insiders, Inefficiency and IOUs
arguments.text: San Francisco has a structural budget problem. Proposition I makes it worse. City Hall keeps using the same playbook: take taxpayer dollars, lock them into specials slush funds, create permanent spending commitments - and leave taxpayers with the bill. This ballot is chockfull of flawed measures - The foreclosure tax. The Housing Trust Fund. Now Proposition I. Different names. Same City Hall shell game. This time, the sales pitch is “affordable housing and “social housing”. Who could be against that? That’s the trick. Follow the money. Prop I continues and expands a slush fund for non-profit programs with no accountability, no oversight and no guarantee that it will build housing. Prop I guarantees a stream of public money for nonprofits and programs without guaranteeing taxpayers what they’ll get for it. No maximum taxpayer cost per unit. No meaningful construction-cost ceiling. No minimum number of units that must be delivered. No requirement to choose the most cost-effective solution. That’s a great deal for the developers, consultants, nonprofits and other interests feeding at the affordable-housing trough. It’s a lousy deal for taxpayers. Prop I even allows City Hall to borrow against this revenue and use it to repay debt. Earmark the money. Spend it. Borrow against it. Then come back to taxpayers when the General Fund runs short. That’s not fiscal responsibility. That’s a racket taxpayers can’t afford. San Francisco cannot tax, earmark and borrow its way out of a structural deficit. Before City Hall locks away another stream of taxpayer dollars, demand results from the billions it already spends. Taxpayers are not City Hall’s ATM! Stop the spending slush fund racket. Stop the budget shell game. Vote NO on Proposition I!

proposal.value: Proposition I would dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance. Specifically, the measure would: Transfer Tax For properties with a sales price or value between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000: • Reduce the current transfer tax from 5.5% to 2.75% • Impose a new transfer tax of 2.75% For properties with a sales price or value at $25,000,000 or more: • Reduce the transfer tax from 6% to 3% • Impose a new transfer tax of 3% This measure will not increase the tax rate on the transfer of any property above what is charged today. The same exemptions and tax reductions from the current transfer tax would still apply to the new transfer tax. The new transfer tax would also exempt the first sale of certain multifamily real estate if it is sold within 5 years of completion of new residential units. Tax Revenue Spending The City could spend revenue from the new transfer tax only on: • At least 60% for affordable housing production, with at least half to social housing developments; • At least 25% towards the acquisition or rehabilitation of affordable housing, with at least 60% to acquisition of existing housing units; and • At least 10% to tenant stabilization/homeless prevention programs, with at least half to eviction defense and prevention; The Board could only change the transfer tax consistent with the purpose of the tax. All other changes would require voter approval. Proposition I would approve an unlimited number of new affordable housing units for low-income households funded by revenue from the new transfer tax. Proposition I would require the City to submit annual reports to the Board and Mayor on the use of the new tax revenue. Proposition I would increase the City’s spending limit for four years.

way_it_is_now.value: The City collects a transfer tax when most real estate changes hands. The tax rates depend on the property’s sales price or value and the two highest tax rates are: • 5.5% for properties between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000, and • 6% for properties at $25,000,000 or more. Some real estate transfers are exempt from the tax or are subject to reduced rates. Revenues generated from the transfer tax may be spent for any governmental purpose. The Board of Supervisors (Board) may amend, reduce, suspend, or repeal the transfer tax without voter approval. Voters must approve any increase of the transfer tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
